models.name: Model A — Night-Earned Attestation ("We ran a night together")
models.mechanic: A vouch can only be given to someone you have verifiably shared a real night with: the app checks co-attendance (same Pool meet or event, geofenced check-in at the same venue, overlapping time window) before the vouch option even appears. The vouch is offered in the post-night flow (the morning-after recap), is one-directional, public ("vouched by Maya — 3 nights together"), and carries the evidence inline: number of co-attended nights, venues, dates. No co-attendance, no vouch button — strangers and internet-only contacts structurally cannot vouch. This is the artifact's "friends are earned, not added" principle extended to reputation: the graph edge and the trust edge are the same verified real-world event.
models.incentives: Strongly incentivises the behaviour Func's thesis actually optimises for — closed loops (invite → accept → attended). To build reputation you must go out, with people, repeatedly; reputation becomes a byproduct of the success metric rather than a separate grind. It also makes the post-night recap a habitual surface (Partiful's after-party lesson) and gives new users a clear, fair on-ramp: one good night with one group starts your record. Weakness: it creates volume pressure — people who go out constantly accumulate vouches regardless of conduct quality, so it can drift from "trusted" toward "prolific".
models.abuseVectors: (1) Check-in farming: two groups repeatedly "meeting" at a free venue to mint co-attendance, or GPS spoofing to fake presence. (2) Volume inflation: heavy-going-out cliques mass-vouching each other every weekend, turning the signal into an activity counter. (3) Reciprocity courtesy: the post-night prompt shown to both parties simultaneously produces Airbnb-style mutual 5-star inflation — everyone vouches everyone to be polite. (4) Popularity contest: large groups generate more edges per night than small ones, structurally advantaging extroverted big-crew users. (5) Exclusion is mild here (anyone can earn), but a cold-start user with no crew still can't begin.
models.mitigations: Diminishing returns per relationship (the 1st vouch from a person counts fully; their repeat vouches only refresh recency, never stack). Per-night cap: you may vouch at most 1–2 people per night, forcing selection rather than blanket courtesy. Anti-spoof: attendance requires two independent signals (geofence + the other group's confirmation of the meet, or a scanned event ticket). Delay + blind reveal: vouches given in the recap are hidden for 48h and never shown as "pending" to the other side, blunting reciprocity; algorithmically discount perfectly-mutual pairs and dense pairwise rings (per the Lobsters/eBay lessons). Show vouch *sources diversity* (distinct groups, distinct venues) rather than raw count.
models.externalValue: Because every vouch is anchored to a verifiable event (time, venue, co-attending group), the attestation is evidence-backed in a way a LinkedIn endorsement never was. External path: a "night record" that venues and event organisers can trust for guest-list fast-track ("12 verified nights, vouched by 9 distinct groups, zero incidents"), and later a portable proof-of-conduct for other IRL-social products (Timeleft/Thursday-style apps, university societies) — the credential asserts a concrete fact pattern, not an opinion score.

models.name: Model B — Scarce Slots ("Your List" — transferable standing attestations)
models.mechanic: Every member holds a small fixed number of vouch slots (e.g. 5), unlocked gradually by tenure (Lobsters-style seasoning: none in your first ~8 weeks / first 3 attended nights). Occupying a slot is a standing state, not a one-off event: "Jordan has Maya on his list." Slots are reassignable but moving one is deliberate and rate-limited (e.g. one reassignment per month) and the removal is visible to the removed person. Your profile shows both directions: who you hold slots for, and who holds slots for you — the full graph is public, like Lobsters' invite tree. A vouch here means the strongest possible statement: "of everyone I know on Func, this is one of the five I put my name behind."
models.incentives: Scarcity does the semantic work: because slots are precious, each vouch is genuinely considered, and being on someone's list feels meaningful — closer to "I'll put my name on the door list for you" than a like. It creates healthy deliberation and makes high-standing people's slots aspirational. Perverse incentives: slots become social currency, which is exactly what makes them dangerous — people feel pressure to allocate slots to close friends regardless of conduct (measuring intimacy, not trustworthiness), removing someone becomes a friendship-ending social event, and newcomers face a chicken-and-egg wait for a scarce slot to open.
models.abuseVectors: (1) Secondary market: the private-tracker lesson — once scarce vouches gate real access (Pool joins, events, venue lists), they get sold or traded ("£20 for a slot"); this is the single most predictable failure. (2) Clique lock-up: friend groups fill each other's slots on day one and the graph fossilises into closed rings — scarcity plus homophily equals a velvet rope, the exact architecture the artifact critique rejected. (3) Coercion: "put me on your list or we're not friends" — scarce social collateral weaponises friendship (the microfinance anthropology finding). (4) Popularity contests around high-status members' open slots. (5) Sybil pressure is low (slots are scarce) but exclusion pressure is the highest of all four models.
models.mitigations: Never let slots be the only path to anything (Pool must always have a mutuals/verification alternative — "vouch OR 2 mutuals", as the artifact itself gated it). Make trading self-defeating: slots are non-detachable from the relationship — a slot-vouch only counts if co-attendance history exists between the pair (importing Model A's gate), so a sold slot to a stranger is visibly hollow and algorithmically worthless. Public graph + tree consequences deter rings (if your slot-holder is banned for serious misconduct, the event is visible on your profile). Soften removals: slots silently expire after 12 months without a shared night, so pruning is the system's fault, not the friend's. Cap the share of slots that can point inside your own everyday group to force graph reach.
models.externalValue: Scarcity is the property outsiders instinctively understand — "only five people have this from him" translates cleanly to the offline referent (a promoter's list). External path: venues honour "listed by a resident regular" for entry perks; a member's list functions as a portable letter of introduction between city scenes ("held a slot from three Manchester hosts for 14 months"). But its external value is also its biggest liability: the more it's worth outside, the stronger the black-market and exclusion pressure — external use would need to stay perk-level (queue skip), never access-level (entry denial).

models.name: Model C — Role-Scoped Vouches ("Shows up" / "Great host" / "Good with new people" / "Looks out for the group")
models.mechanic: Vouches are typed, not generic. A small fixed vocabulary (4–6 conduct verbs, each with concrete semantics): Shows up (was committed, arrived, stayed), Great host (organised the night, handled the venue/table), Good with new people (made the other group welcome at a Pool meet), Looks out for people (got everyone home safe, handled a bad moment well). Each type is only offerable in the context that could have evidenced it — "Great host" only to the night's actual host, "Good with new people" only after a Pool meet between previously-unconnected groups, "Shows up" only against a real RSVP that was honoured. Profiles display earned types with counts and sources ("Shows up ×9 · from 6 groups"), replacing any single reputation number.
models.incentives: Names and rewards the specific behaviours Func's liquidity depends on: flake-resistance ("Shows up" directly attacks the Pool's riskiest assumption — will groups honour invites), hosting supply, and welcomingness to strangers (the exact opposite of clique behaviour — the only reputation system of the four that actively incentivises openness). Concrete single-meaning semantics is the PGP lesson applied: users never have to interpret what a vouch "means". It also creates multiple valid ways to be reputable — the quiet reliable friend and the charismatic host earn different, equally legible standing — which resists a one-dimensional popularity ladder. Weakness as a standalone: no cost to the giver, so each individual vouch is cheap and the system alone can inflate like endorsements did.
models.abuseVectors: (1) Endorsement inflation: typed but costless clicks drift toward courtesy confetti — counts balloon, distribution compresses, LinkedIn redux. (2) Category gaming: hosts fishing for "Great host" by spamming low-effort nights; RSVP-then-attend farming of "Shows up" at trivial free events. (3) Reciprocal type-swapping ("you badge my hosting, I badge your vibes"). (4) Absence reading: a profile with zero "Looks out for people" invites unfair negative inference (the Airbnb missing-review problem). (5) Scope creep pressure: users will lobby for vibe/attractiveness/status categories ("life of the party"), which reintroduces the popularity contest and, at the venue-facing edge, the discrimination machine the door-culture research warns about.
models.mitigations: Import cost from the other models: each type offerable only from verified context (Model A's co-attendance gate) and rate-limited per night; voucher-weighting so a "Great host" from an established, multiply-vouched member outweighs ten from fresh accounts (the Ethos mechanic, minus crypto). Lock the vocabulary — conduct verbs only, no vibe/appearance categories, ever; this is the anti-discrimination firewall for any venue-facing use. Show recency-weighted, source-diverse summaries ("from 6 groups, last 90 days") not lifetime counts. Never render absent categories; profiles show what someone has earned, with no empty placeholder rows to read negatively.
models.externalValue: Highest-legibility external artifact of the four, because each type answers a question a real-world counterparty actually asks. "Shows up" is a no-flake score any event organiser, supper club, or five-a-side league understands; "Great host" is a credential venues can use to identify organisers worth courting with table deals (the B2B2C bridge — venues paying to reach proven hosts); "Looks out for people" is the seed of a safety-conduct record that women-first safety features can build on. Because semantics are concrete and behavioural, the credential exports without exporting a ranking of human worth.

models.name: Model D — Stake-Based Standing ("Name on the Door" — voucher shares the consequences)
models.mechanic: Vouching puts your own standing partially on the line, mirroring the promoter's repeated-game accountability from door culture. Every member has a Standing level (fed by verified nights, conduct record, and voucher-weighted vouches received). When you vouch, your standing visibly backs the vouchee — profiles read "backed by Maya (High standing)". Consequences flow both ways along the edge: if someone you back is reported and confirmed for serious misconduct, your vouch auto-revokes, your standing dips, and your vouching privilege is suspended for a period; if your backed people consistently complete good nights, your standing slowly strengthens as a proven judge of character. Vouches are revocable at any time (quietly, with a cooling-off delay). Standing is coarse and non-numeric in UI (bands, not scores) to avoid leaderboard psychology.
models.incentives: This is the model that makes a vouch a costly signal rather than a message: you only back people you'd genuinely answer for, which is precisely the CEO's "meaningful, not a like" bar. It creates a self-policing graph — vouchers screen and quietly counsel their vouchees (the Grameen effect) — which directly subsidises Func's trust-and-safety cost structure, the #4 riskiest assumption (moderation costs at student price points). It rewards good judgment as its own reputational skill. Risks: over-chilling (if the downside feels scary, vouching collapses and the growth loop dies) and anxiety-driven social pressure on vouchees ("don't embarrass me tonight"), the coercive edge microfinance research documents.
models.abuseVectors: (1) Weaponised reporting: rivals file false misconduct reports to slash a whole backing tree — the stake mechanism turns moderation into an attack surface. (2) Standing cartels: high-standing members selling backings (standing becomes literal currency; private-tracker invite markets predict this). (3) Risk-aversion exclusion: rational actors only back demographically similar, already-established people — the stake amplifies homophily and punishes exactly the newcomer-welcoming behaviour the Pool needs. (4) Cascade injustice: one bad actor's confirmed report dents several backers who had no way to foresee it, poisoning friendships (demonetisation-cascade analogue). (5) Sybil insulation: bad actors maintain clean "backer" accounts that never go out.
models.mitigations: Slashing only on *confirmed, serious* violations (safety incidents, verified harassment — human-reviewed), never on flakiness, taste, or one-sided complaints; false-report penalties for the reporter. Cap the dip (a backer loses standing progress, never their own verified-night record — reputational, not existential, per the microfinance calibration). Small backing capacity (3–5 concurrent) so exposure is bounded and deliberate. Newcomer insurance: backing a low-tenure member carries *reduced* downside for their first weeks plus upside if it goes well — explicitly tilting the risk calculus toward on-ramping rather than exclusion. All standing inputs are conduct-and-attendance based, never social-graph size, so cartels can't mint standing without real nights.
models.externalValue: Standing backed by stake is the only variant with genuine external credibility economics: outsiders can trust it because it demonstrably cost something to give and survives an ongoing test (it would have been revoked otherwise) — the same reason a cosigned lease means more than a reference letter. External path: venue partners honour "backed, high-standing" for guest-list and table-hold privileges with real accountability behind it (Func can tell a venue "if this goes wrong, it costs someone identifiable"); long-term, standing bands become a portable trust passport for the IRL-social category. Guardrail: external use must stay perk-granting and conduct-scoped — never an automated velvet rope that denies entry — or it re-imports door-culture discrimination with an algorithmic face.

recommendation.model: Model D — Stake-Based Standing ("Name on the Door"), built on Model A's co-attendance gate and Model C's typed vocabulary; Model B's scarcity adopted only as a capacity cap, never as tradeable slots
recommendation.rationale: The research is unambiguous about what keeps a reputation signal meaningful long-term: scarce, costly, attributable, revocable, and consequential for the giver. Only the stake-based model delivers the last and hardest property — consequence for the giver — which is what separates a vouch from a like and is the exact bar the CEO set. The other models supply necessary preconditions rather than competing answers, so the recommendation is D as the engine with A and C as its gates and grammar: co-attendance gating (A) makes vouches evidence-backed and un-farmable by strangers; the typed conduct vocabulary (C) keeps semantics concrete (the PGP lesson), makes the Pool's key behaviours — showing up, hosting, welcoming strangers — the things reputation is made of, and is the anti-discrimination firewall for any venue-facing use; a small backing capacity imports B's scarcity without tradeable-slot pathology. Strategically, D is also the only model that compounds with Func's business: it subsidises trust-and-safety (self-policing graph attacks riskiest assumption #4), it directly counters Pool flake risk (riskiest assumption #1), and it is the only vouch design a venue can rationally pay to honour, because Func can attach identifiable accountability to every name it puts on a door list — the B2B2C bridge. Its known failure modes (over-chill, homophily amplification, weaponised reports) are the ones with concrete, evidence-backed mitigations — bounded reputational-only downside, newcomer insurance, human-reviewed slashing limited to confirmed serious misconduct — whereas Model B's black-market/exclusion failure mode has no good mitigation once scarcity gates real access (the private-tracker record shows it), and A or C standing alone inflate into activity counters or endorsement confetti. Culturally it is also the right fit: 'I'll put my name on the list for you' is the native idiom of Func's users, imported with door culture's accountability but not its discrimination.
recommendation.prototypeScope: Demo-scope for the Velmont prototype (Expo app at /Users/phoenixbarnes/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/Func./prototype), seed-data driven, no backend: (1) Data: add Vouch {fromId, toId, type: 'shows_up'|'great_host'|'good_with_new_people'|'looks_out', nightId, createdAt} and standing: 'new'|'building'|'solid'|'high' to /prototype/data/types.ts, seed ~20 vouches across existing users in /prototype/data/ with realistic co-attendance references. (2) Profile surfaces: on app/(tabs)/profile.tsx and app/person/[id].tsx, add a standing band chip next to the verified badge, typed-vouch rows with source diversity ('Shows up ×6 · from 4 groups'), and a tappable 'Backed by' row showing backers with their standing — plus the 'backing 2 of 4' capacity indicator on your own profile. (3) The earn moment: a post-night recap screen (link from group/[id].tsx) listing last night's co-attendees with at most 2 vouch selections, typed options contextually filtered (host gets 'Great host'), and copy making the stake explicit: 'Backing puts your name on it. If they let the night down badly, it reflects on you.' (4) The spend moment: in the Pool (app/(tabs)/pool.tsx), gate one seeded stranger-group's invite with 'Backed member or 2 mutuals to join' and show accepting groups the applicants' standing + typed vouches — demonstrating reputation doing something, per the artifact's adopted mechanic. (5) One consequence vignette: a seeded notification/detail state showing a revoked backing after a confirmed report and the backer's standing dip, to make shared consequence legible to pitch audiences. Explicit non-goals for prototype: no real slashing logic, no scores/numbers anywhere in UI (bands only), no venue-facing surface, no reporting flow — those are v1 backend concerns.
